title: Paddle vs Polar
summary: Two true Merchants of Record for software, with different operating histories, pricing structures, and developer-product emphasis.
recommendation: Start with Paddle when mature SaaS operations and enterprise support matter most. Start with Polar when transparent tier choices, developer tooling, usage billing, and built-in benefits better match the product.

differences.first: 5% + $0.50 pay-as-you-go, with custom pricing for larger businesses.
differences.second: 5% + $0.50 Starter plus paid monthly plans that reduce the variable rate.
differences.whyItMatters: Polar exposes self-serve breakpoints; Paddle moves larger sellers toward negotiated terms.

differences.first: Long-established software and SaaS commerce provider.
differences.second: Newer developer-focused platform with an open-source product.
differences.whyItMatters: Risk tolerance and procurement expectations can outweigh individual features.

differences.first: Strong subscription SaaS lifecycle and revenue-recovery tooling.
differences.second: Strong developer products, usage and seat billing, and benefit delivery.
differences.whyItMatters: Choose the platform whose native model resembles your catalog and entitlements.

differences.first: Documents sales across more than 200 countries and territories.
differences.second: Documents global payments with a separate seller-payout country list.
differences.whyItMatters: Buyer reach and seller eligibility are separate questions.

differences.first: Offers sales-assisted and custom migration services.
differences.second: Publishes developer migration documentation and APIs.
differences.whyItMatters: Large subscriber migrations usually require written provider commitments, regardless of tooling.

implementation.summary: Both providers remove substantial tax and billing operations. Polar is especially compact for developer products because its simplest path is a reusable checkout link and it bundles framework adapters, a customer portal, and automated benefits; Paddle favors a broader, mature SaaS billing workflow.

first.label: Frontend only
first.detail: Paddle documents a five-minute overlay checkout using Paddle.js, a client-side token, and a price ID.

second.label: No code
second.detail: Create a long-lived Checkout Link in the dashboard and share it directly; no server or custom payment UI is required.

first.label: Paddle.js
first.detail: Load Paddle.js and open or render a provider-managed overlay or inline checkout.

second.label: HTML snippet
second.detail: A link attribute and script can open the Polar embed; a JavaScript package is available for programmatic control.

first.label: Webhook sync
first.detail: Production SaaS uses lifecycle webhooks to provision access and keep subscription state in sync.

second.label: Adapters + webhooks
second.detail: Official framework adapters create checkout and verify typed webhooks; the CLI can relay events during local development.

first.label: Merchant built
first.detail: Your application normally maps Paddle transactions and subscriptions to its own product entitlements.

second.label: Partly built in
second.detail: Benefits can automate license keys, downloads, GitHub or Discord access, credits, and simple feature flags; custom access still uses API or webhooks.

first.label: Bundled
first.detail: Trials, proration, upgrades, dunning, cancellation flows, and a customer portal are native.

second.label: Bundled
second.detail: Recurring and usage pricing, retries, grace periods, plan changes, seats, and a hosted portal are native.

first.label: Strong
first.detail: Separate sandbox, test transactions, webhook simulator, SDKs, and an end-to-end quickstart.

second.label: Strong
second.detail: Isolated sandbox, typed SDKs, framework adapters, Standard Webhooks, and a local webhook tunnel in the Polar CLI.

first.label: Included
first.detail: Paddle's hosted portal covers subscriptions, invoices, payment methods, and cancellations.

second.label: Included
second.detail: Polar's always-available portal covers subscriptions, invoices, benefits, seats, usage, cancellations, and payment recovery.

first.label: SaaS oriented
first.detail: More mature billing and retention surfaces, within Paddle's checkout and Merchant of Record constraints.

second.label: Developer oriented
second.detail: A compact hosted experience with easy embeds and APIs; the hosted customer portal has intentionally limited branding.

scenarios.when: You run established subscription SaaS and need a mature operating partner.
scenarios.reason: Paddle's product and support model is oriented around scaled SaaS billing operations.

scenarios.when: You sell developer tooling with usage, seats, or entitlement benefits.
scenarios.reason: Polar makes these models unusually central to the product.

scenarios.when: Your decision is mainly cost at a known monthly volume.
scenarios.reason: Its published plan ladder makes self-serve breakpoints easier to model; still include additional fees.
